https://www.dw.com/en/far-right-afd-puts.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MYVA AfD leader Alice Weidel is calling on Merz to stop assistance to Ukraine in its fight against the Russian invasion Image: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS Advertisement German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is standing firm on military aid for Ukraine in its war with Russia . "We support Ukraine, and we will continue to support her, because she is also defending our freedom," Merz said on September 9 during a debate in the Bundestag , Germany's lower house of parliament. He was reacting to Alternative for Germany (AfD) co-leader Alice Weidel , who had urged him to "finally start pushing for peace talks, like the US is doing." US President Donald Trump has indicated that he would make far-reaching concessions to Russia at such negotiations; critics in Germany have described that as dictated peace. On the topic of high energy prices in Germany, Weidel said, "We need cheap natural gas from Russia. That is what we will work toward." She insinuated that the Ukrainian government was responsible for blowing up the Nord Stream gas pipelines between Russia and Germany in September 2022. "They continue to reward the suspected masterminds of the attack in Kyiv with billion-dollar payments at the expense of Germany." A Ukrainian sabotage team is suspected to be behind the attack. Merz and Weidel clash in parliament after AfD election win To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video How pro-Russia the AfD is, despite its invasion of Ukraine, was shown clearly by its lawmaker Jürgen Koegel during the debate. He spoke of "valued President Vladimir Putin ," who posed no threat of war to NATO . East-west division in Germany over Ukraine aid The AfD's position on the war in Ukraine is nothing new. However, since winning the state parliament election in Saxony-Anhalt on September 6 by a large margin, gaining almost 44% of the vote, it has expressed it even more vehemently. Combining the votes for the AfD, the socialist Left Party and the populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), about 60% of voters in Saxony-Anhalt chose parties that either oppose support for Ukraine or are skeptical of it. According to one survey, citizens' concerns about peace in Europe influenced their votes. Those surveyed named this topic as their second-most important, after "social security" and far ahead of "immigration" or "environment and climate." In addition, there is the result of an ARD Deutschlandtrend survey conducted shortly before the election. It showed an east-west divide on the question of military support for Ukraine. About 39% of western Germans (from the area which was West Germany prior to reunification) thought military assistance went too far, while it was 54% for eastern Germans — that is, people who live in the area which used to be the communist German Democratic Republic (GDR/DDR). "The course that the German federal government is taking on Ukraine does not have majority support in the east," Johannes Varwick, a political scientist at the Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg in Saxony-Anhalt, told DW. "I would not describe that as 'pro-Russia'; it comes from the desire to focus more on diplomacy rather than delivering ever more weapons to fuel a war which Ukraine cannot win." Fear in Germany of Russian threats On September 2, the German government blamed Russia for a failed attack with an armed drone in early August at Leipzig airport, a key hub for military aid to Ukraine. Putin spoke of a "grave error," Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov even called the accusation the "start of a real war." The exchange of verbal blows marked a new level of escalation in an already tense relationship. According to the latest ARD Deutschlandtrend survey, most Germans (56%) see themselves currently either strongly or very strongly threatened by Russia. But it also showed that eastern Germans and AfD voters feel less threatened by Russia. The election results in Saxony-Anhalt also seem to reflect this. Political scientist Sven Leunig from the Friedrich Schiller University Jena in the state of Thuringia has his own take on the reaction of eastern Germans, especially after the Leipzig incident. "It is less a fundamental rejection of support for Ukraine, more a reaction based on fear," Leunig said. "They want to keep out of the conflict, so as not to be drawn further into it. That of course strengthens parties like the AfD, BSW and Left, who accommodate these sentiments." Support for Ukraine is also coming under pressure for another reason. According to the AfD and BSW, the money Ukraine receives could be better spent on Germany's stretched social services. AfD lawmaker Gottfried Curio, for example, accused the German government of cutting social benefits and raising taxes "to keep on giving billions to foreign countries," to finance "foreign wars" such as in Ukraine. Germany seeks extradition of Nord Stream 2 bombing suspect To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Support for Ukraine is crumbling, but slowly Chancellor Merz still believes he has political and public backing for his course. During the Bundestag debate, this was his response to the AfD's suggestion of resuming energy deliveries from Russia and ending German support for Ukraine: "This path that you depict is not supported by the majority in the German parliament and it is also not supported by the majority of the population of the Federal Republic of Germany. We will defend our freedom, also in the future." But support for Ukraine, as shown in ARD Deutschlandtrend surveys over the years, is becoming less favored by the public. The share of people who think military support goes too far is growing, slowly but steadily, and is now 42%. Leunig thinks the German government is not yet under pressure to reconsider its Ukraine policy: it still has "clear support" for the current course. "Plus, the threat coming from Russia is also becoming widely recognized. Of course, if public support weakens in the long-term, the government will have to react to that." Is Ukraine 'another Afghanistan'? His colleague Johannes Varwick, on the other hand, advises a course correction now, but not so much due to the mood in Germany: "Yes, we should stand with Ukraine, but standing by Ukraine does not mean fueling a futile war of attrition without a viable political strategy. That runs Ukraine into the ground, even if it is portrayed as 'pro-Ukraine'." Critics have drawn parallels to Western intervention in Afghanistan , which after 20 years, billions of dollars spent and about 3500 western soldiers killed, ended with the Taliban retaking power. But Leunig sees it differently. "I think both cases are not identical. In Afghanistan there was a direct military intervention by Western countries with ground and air forces. In Ukraine, the support is supplying weapons. But the public fear that the war will drag on for a long time, in this there is of course a parallel to Afghanistan, and that in the end Ukraine might still have to give up." So far, however, there is no sign that the German government is rethinking its position. During a recent (September 10) visit from NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Berlin, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said, "Germany will stay the course during this time," despite the domestic debate. McGuinty, Minister of National Defence, at the International Defence Industry Exhibition (MSPO), held from September 8 to 11, 2026, in Kielce, Poland, to promote Canada's defence industry, as well as to deepen Canada's trade relationships with Poland and across Europe. Canada and Poland are strengthening ties in defence, trade, advanced technologies and energy security, and, as North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) Allies, are united in supporting collective defence and transatlantic security. Minister Sidhu kicked off his visit to Poland in Warsaw by meeting with Andrzej Domański, Minister of Finance and Economy. They discussed opportunities to expand Canada-Poland commercial collaboration in priority sectors such as defence, energy and aerospace. Minister Sidhu also met with both Miłosz Motyka, Minister of Energy, and Wojciech Wrochna, Plenipotentiary for Strategic Energy Infrastructure and Secretary of State at the Ministry of Energy, to champion Canada as one of the world's most reliable suppliers of clean energy. At the meeting, Minister Sidhu promoted Canada's successful nuclear energy program, based on the unique heavy water natural uranium reactor system, known as CANDU (CANada Deuterium Uranium). In Kielce, Minister Sidhu and Minister McGuinty attended MSPO 2026, where they met with defence industry leaders and formally opened the Canada Pavilion together with Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, Poland's Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence. As this year's lead nation, Canada is showcasing its defence and security capabilities, innovation and industrial expertise at MSPO, one of Europe's premier defence exhibitions. At MSPO 2026, more than 20 memorandums of understanding were signed, supporting future industry collaboration in the growing defence sector. This momentum is also reflected in trade figures, with Canadian defence exports to Europe increasing by 56% in the last year. With a Team Canada approach, Canada's presence at MSPO 2026 included more than 200 organizations and nearly 500 delegates from Canada's industry and all levels of government, making it the country's largest defence and security business mission worldwide and the largest business delegation Canada has ever brought to Poland. This included 20 economic development organizations from across the country, which participated in more than 200 pre-arranged meetings with international companies to promote Canada as a competitive destination for investment and attract job-creating investment. The ministers' participation highlighted Canada's commitment to expanding commercial and industrial cooperation with partners across Central and Eastern Europe. Canada's involvement at MSPO supports Canada's broader Defence Industrial Strategy, as well as efforts to diversify and strengthen international partnerships and deepen defence industrial cooperation with European partners, including through Canada's participation in the EU's Security Action for Europe (SAFE) initiative. These efforts are also reinforced by Canada's Strategic Exports Office, which helps Canadian businesses pursue major export opportunities in strategic sectors, including defence and security. Quotes "Over 200 Canadian companies joined us at MSPO in Poland, our largest ever delegation, in a market where our defence exports have grown over 300%. I saw firsthand how CAE, a company that supports over 4,500 jobs here in Canada, is partnering with WB Group to unlock new opportunities in Poland as we grow our presence here. That kind of momentum across our defence sector will diversify our trade while creating 125,000 more jobs for Canadians over the next decade." - Maninder Sidhu, Minister of International Trade "Canada's defence industry is central to our security, our sovereignty and our economic strength. At MSPO, we are showing our Allies that Canada is ready to do more: to build more at home, deepen industrial cooperation and deliver the capabilities our collective defence demands. As NATO Allies, Canada and Poland are investing in a stronger, more-resilient defence industrial base that creates opportunities for Canadian workers and businesses while making our Alliance stronger." - David J. McGuinty, Minister of National Defence Quick facts The MSPO is Europe's third-largest defence and security trade show, and the flagship defence event in Central and Eastern Europe. Held annually, the 2026 exhibition was the largest to date and hosted more than 40,000 visitors, more than 1,200 exhibitors and more than 60 official delegations. In 2025, Poland was Canada's fourth-largest military goods and technology export market and the second largest in Europe. Canada's defence military goods and technology exports to Poland were valued at $216.8 million, up 319% from 2024. More than 60 Canadian companies successfully operate in Poland. Since the 2017 provisional application of the Canada-European Union Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), two-way merchandise trade between Poland and Canada has doubled, and was up 33% from 2024. Canada was the first NATO Ally to ratify Poland's accession to NATO in 1998. Today, Canadian and Polish troops serve side by side in the NATO Multinational Brigade Latvia. Poland was a key supporter of Canada's participation in the EU's SAFE defence financing program, making Canada the first non-European country able to participate.

Photograph: Bim/Getty Images Paris Tall, dark and hated: plan to renovate ‘Paris’s ugliest building’ put on hold Tour Montparnasse modernisation project at a standstill after clashes over pricing and other issues Angelique Chrisafis in Paris Fri 25 Sep 2026 07.25 EDT Last modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 10.36 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google It has been called a carbuncle on the Paris skyline, a sombre skyscraper where visitors to its viewing platform often joke that the city looks better when you can’t see the building itself. The much-maligned Tour Montparnasse, a lone, dark monolith with tinted windows rising above a historic neighbourhood in the south of the city, is once again at the centre of controversy after its long-awaited renovation was halted this week because of disagreements between its many private co-owners. The tower, which opened in 1973, is the tallest skyscraper in inner-city Paris and is also considered its ugliest building. View image in fullscreen Paris’s tallest inner-city skyscraper is due to undergo a massive structural transition. Photograph: Frédéric Vielcanet/Alamy For more than a decade, plans have been thrashed out to overhaul the building and brighten its looming presence and modernise the area around it. Architects had planned to entirely refit the 210-metre structure with a new glass exterior, adding vegetation throughout, with a garden terrace on the 16th floor and an agricultural greenhouse at the top. The plans included a hotel on three floors of the 59-storey building, as well as new office and leisure spaces. But alongside a significant operation to remove asbestos, the estimated price of the project more than doubled to €800m (£688m). The building’s private co-owners, which include French investment funds and insurers, met this week for a final vote on the start of a first phase of renovation, with asbestos removal, interior stripping and a partial facade removal. After clashes over plans and pricing, more than three-quarters of the co-owners voted against the project. It was the last opportunity to launch the project before the building permit granted for the tower’s renovation expires at the end of November. There are now concerns that the building, which has been emptied and closed for renovation, will loom deserted. This summer, fire officers intervened after bits of glass fell off the building and landed on the street below, although no one was hurt. View image in fullscreen A design for the renovation of the Tour Montparnasse. Illustration: RPBW “Everyone needs to come to their senses,” said Philippe Goujon, the rightwing mayor of Paris’s 15th district where the tower is located. He told Agence France-Presse: “I cannot accept seeing a project that took 10 years to develop thrown away, or allowing this world-renowned landmark to fall into neglect.” Four of the co-owners who still want a renovation, including the tycoon Xavier Niel, said in a joint statement: “We would like all the co-owners, financial partners and public authorities to meet soon to examine all the solutions to transform the Montparnasse Tower.” Some co-owners hope that a new, scaled-down project could be agreed upon. View image in fullscreen Many commercial spaces within the tower have been left derelict. Photograph: Abaca Press/Alamy Separately, the architect Renzo Piano has been tasked with overhauling the shopping centre beneath the tower and other buildings nearby, opening up new pedestrian spaces and moving from grey concrete to a greener, planted space. Local officials want to avoid delays to that project if the tower’s renovation stalls. The office of the Socialist mayor of Paris, Emmanuel Grégoire , said it wanted “an alternative solution to be proposed” so the site does not stay at a standstill. Opposition councillors on the left have suggested the “obsolete” tower should instead come down and be replaced by a park that would have a cooling effect during summer heatwaves. https://www.politico.eu/article/french-p.text: PARIS — France’s anti-terrorism prosecutor is investigating a shooting near Paris which killed at least one person Friday morning as a possible act of hate-motivated terror. “The National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor’s Office has taken up this case and opened an investigation,” it said in a statement, adding that the suspect has been placed in custody. The office is investigating charges including murder and attempted murder “in connection with a terrorist enterprise, where the acts were committed on the basis of actual or perceived membership of a specific race, ethnicity, nation or religion.” Advertisement Advertisement Earlier in the day, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu announced on X that at least one person had been killed and four others injured in a shooting in Trappes, a suburb west of Paris with a lower socioeconomic status and a large Muslim community. A 12-year-old was among those injured, the mayor of nearby town La Verrière told reporters . “The main focus will obviously be on identifying the perpetrator’s motives — what drove him to attempt to carry out a massacre … to target our communities,” Trappes Mayor Ali Rabeh said on French broadcaster BFM . “Our thoughts are with the victims, their families, and all the residents of Yvelines. During this terrible ordeal, the nation stands with them,” President Emmanuel Macron said on social media . Marine Le Pen, the front-running far-right candidate for next year’s presidential election slammed the killing as “a barbaric act whose motives must be determined, and of which those responsible must be severely punished.” “Racism kills,” Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leading left-wing candidate for next year’s election. “In the face of this heinous crime, all human beings are reminded that they are alike as they see themselves united in horror and outrage.” Center-right candidate Edouard Philippe said “terrorism must be fought relentlessly, with absolute determination” and that “the investigation will have to determine the motives of the perpetrator of this despicable act.” This is a developing story.
